title: Unlimited password brute force against any account by rotating X-Forwarded-For (per-IP limiter and per-account anomaly detection both bypassed, no lockout)
scenario: Anonymous attacker guesses a victim's password until it works, undetected and unthrottled.
evidence: 30 wrong-password logins against one account, each from a different spoofed X-Forwarded-For -> all 401, none 429/403; a 31st login with the correct password -> 200. Same IP without rotation hits 429 after 20 (limiter is purely per-IP).
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Brute force / credential stuffing › rotating X-Forwarded-For does NOT let an attacker brute force a victim's password unthrottled; › after a burst of failed logins the correct password should not simply keep working
cause: server/auth.ts:110-114 authLimiter is express-rate-limit keyed on req.ip, and with app.set('trust proxy',1) (server/auth.ts:96) req.ip is the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For, so each attempt looks like a new IP. There is no per-account limiter and no account lockout. The anomaly detector (server/services/anomaly-detector.ts:33-46) does count by userId, but its autoAction is only 'account_flagged' and nothing freezes/locks the account, so guessing continues.
fix: Add a per-account login limiter (keyGenerator on normalized req.body.username) and a progressive lockout/step-up after N failures per account; set express-rate-limit trustProxy/keyGenerator to a single trusted hop (or use the leftmost non-trusted XFF entry) so a client cannot mint a fresh IP per request.

title: Registration and password-change rate limits are also per-IP and bypassed by X-Forwarded-For rotation (mass account creation; current-password brute force with a stolen session)
scenario: Attacker creates unlimited accounts, or brute-forces the current password to hijack a session into a permanent takeover, by rotating X-Forwarded-For.
evidence: 15 registrations from 15 spoofed IPs -> all 201 (0x 429); 10 wrong currentPassword attempts on PATCH /api/profile/password from rotating IPs -> all 400 (0x 429). Same IP: register 429 after 5, password-change 429 after 5.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Brute force / credential stuffing › registration is rate-limited even when X-Forwarded-For is rotated; › current-password brute force on PATCH /api/profile/password is throttled despite X-Forwarded-For rotation
cause: server/auth.ts:116-127 strictAuthLimiter and passwordChangeLimiter are express-rate-limit with the default req.ip key; trust proxy makes req.ip the spoofable X-Forwarded-For (server/auth.ts:96).
fix: Same as ATK-AUTH-1: fix the proxy/key handling so limits key on the real connecting IP; additionally key the password-change limiter on the authenticated user id, not the IP.

title: Login, register and logout have no CSRF protection (login CSRF, forced logout)
scenario: A malicious page logs a victim's browser into an attacker-controlled account (login CSRF) or forcibly logs the victim out.
evidence: POST /api/login with no x-csrf-token -> 200 + session cookie; POST /api/register no token -> 201; POST /api/logout no token -> 200. (PATCH /api/profile correctly returns 403 for a foreign/absent token.)
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: CSRF and CORS › POST /api/login requires a CSRF token; › POST /api/register requires a CSRF token; › POST /api/logout requires a CSRF token
cause: server/auth.ts:248/384/432 register these routes inside setupAuth, which runs (server/routes/index.ts:146) before the global app.use('/api', validateCsrf) at server/routes/index.ts:225, and they do not call validateCsrf themselves (unlike /api/profile at server/auth.ts:468). server/index.ts also accepts urlencoded bodies so a plain cross-site <form> works without preflight.
fix: Add validateCsrf to the login/register/logout handlers (the client already fetches /api/csrf-token first), or move the global CSRF middleware before setupAuth's routes.

title: CORS reflects any Origin (including 'null') with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
scenario: Any web page (or a sandboxed/data: document) reads a logged-in victim's authenticated API responses cross-origin.
evidence: GET /api/user with Origin: https://evil.example -> ACAO: https://evil.example, ACAC: true; Origin: null -> ACAO: null, ACAC: true.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: CSRF and CORS › CORS does not reflect an arbitrary Origin with credentials; › CORS does not grant credentialed access to the 'null' origin
cause: server/index.ts cors({ origin: true, credentials: true }) reflects every Origin. SameSite=Lax currently keeps the cookie off most cross-site fetches, but the reflection means any same-site variant can read /api/csrf-token and /api/user.
fix: cors({ origin: <explicit allow-list from env>, credentials: true }); the SPA is same-origin and needs no CORS at all. Never allow the 'null' origin with credentials.

title: IP/device bans do not cover the auth routes: a banned client can still register and log in
scenario: A banned abuser re-enters the platform at will by creating a fresh account and logging in from the banned IP/device.
evidence: Admin creates an active IP ban for 10.66.6.66. From that IP: GET /api/feed/communities -> 403 IP_BANNED (ban works on feature routes), but POST /api/register -> 201 and POST /api/login -> 200.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Banned / frozen account bypass › an IP-banned attacker cannot register a new account; › an IP-banned attacker cannot log in
cause: banCheckMiddleware is mounted at server/routes/index.ts:149, AFTER setupAuth (server/routes/index.ts:146) which already registered /api/register, /api/login, /api/logout, /api/profile*. Express runs route handlers in registration order, so these auth routes answer before banCheckMiddleware ever runs.
fix: Run banCheckMiddleware before the auth routes (it only needs req.user, so place it right after passport.session() inside setupAuth), or move the auth routes into a router mounted after the ban check.

title: A frozen account can still change its own profile and password
scenario: A moderator freezes an abusive account, but the user keeps editing their profile and can even rotate their password.
evidence: Admin sets isFrozen=1. POST /api/comments -> 403 ACCOUNT_FROZEN, but PATCH /api/profile {bio} -> 200 and PATCH /api/profile/password {currentPassword,newPassword} -> 200.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Banned / frozen account bypass › a frozen account cannot change its profile; › a frozen account cannot change its password
cause: Same ordering bug as ATK-AUTH-5: PATCH /api/profile and /api/profile/password are registered in setupAuth (server/auth.ts:468,504) before banCheckMiddleware (server/routes/index.ts:149), which holds the freeze check (server/middleware/ban-check.ts:63-74).
fix: Run banCheckMiddleware before these routes (see ATK-AUTH-5).

title: Changing the password does not invalidate the user's other sessions
scenario: After an attacker steals a session cookie, the victim changes their password but the attacker's session keeps working — takeover persists.
evidence: Two sessions on one account. Session A changes the password -> 200. Session B GET /api/user -> 200 (still authenticated).
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Session attacks › changing the password invalidates the user's other sessions
cause: server/auth.ts:520-524 only updates the password hash; existing rows in the session store (passport.user = id) stay valid and deserializeUser (server/auth.ts:213) checks no password/version stamp.
fix: On password change, delete the user's other sessions from the store (where passport.user = id and sessionID != current), or store passwordChangedAt/sessionVersion and reject stale sessions in deserializeUser; regenerate the current session id.

title: bcrypt 72-byte truncation: passwords sharing their first 72 bytes are interchangeable
scenario: A user with a long passphrase can be logged into by any string that shares only the first 72 bytes, shrinking the effective secret.
evidence: Register with ('A'*72 + '-REAL-TAIL'). Login with ('A'*72 + '-COMPLETELY-DIFFERENT-TAIL') -> 200. Control differing within the first 72 bytes -> 401.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Password policy › bcrypt 72-byte truncation: two passwords sharing the first 72 bytes are NOT interchangeable
cause: server/auth.ts:29-31 hashPassword = bcrypt.hash(password,12) and :33-42 comparePasswords feed the raw password straight to bcrypt, which only considers the first 72 bytes. shared/schema.ts:529 allows passwords up to 128 chars, so tails beyond byte 72 are silently ignored.
fix: Pre-hash the password before bcrypt (e.g. base64(sha256(password))) so the full length contributes, or reject passwords longer than 72 bytes at validation.

title: registration_enabled setting is never enforced — registration cannot actually be disabled
scenario: An admin turns off 'Allow Registration' (e.g. invite-only or during an incident), but anonymous users keep creating accounts.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Maintenance mode and registration-closed bypass › disabling registration (registration_enabled=false) actually blocks new accounts
cause: The register handler (server/auth.ts:248-382) never reads the 'registration_enabled' setting; the only references are server/services/settings.ts:98 (default) and server/routes/index.ts:205 where it is merely exposed via /api/public/settings. No server-side enforcement exists.
fix: In POST /api/register, early-return 403 when SettingsService.get('users','registration_enabled') is false (allow staff/invite flows as intended).

title: Maintenance mode fails to block registration and profile/password edits
scenario: While admins believe the site is closed for maintenance, non-staff users still register and change their profile/password.
evidence: maintenance_mode=true: GET /api/feed/communities -> 503 (blocked), but POST /api/register -> 201, PATCH /api/profile -> 200, PATCH /api/profile/password -> 200.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Maintenance mode and registration-closed bypass › maintenance mode blocks new registrations; › maintenance mode blocks non-admin profile and password edits
cause: The maintenance middleware is mounted at server/routes/index.ts:157, AFTER setupAuth (:146). The register/profile/password routes are already registered, so they answer before the maintenance check runs — its explicit /api/register 503 branch (server/routes/index.ts:167-172) is unreachable.
fix: Move the maintenance middleware (and the ban check) before setupAuth's routes, or enforce maintenance/ban/registration inside those handlers.

title: Public profile exposes other users' moderation and internal fields
scenario: Anyone scraping /api/users/:username learns who is frozen/shadow-banned and other internal state.
evidence: Anonymous GET /api/users/<frozen user> -> JSON includes isFrozen:1, isShadowBanned, emailVerified, karma, (and freezeReason/adminGroupId when set). Email is now stripped, moderation state is not.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: User enumeration › public profile does not expose moderation/internal fields
cause: server/routes/users.ts:299 destructures out only password and email and spreads the whole row (…publicUser), so is_frozen/is_shadow_banned/freeze_reason/admin_group_id/email_verified/karma all leak.
fix: Build the public profile from an explicit allow-list (id, username, displayName, bio, location, website, avatarUrl, coverUrl, role, verified, karma?, createdAt, isPrivate).

title: User search leaks other users' email addresses
scenario: Any logged-in user harvests email addresses of others via the search endpoint.
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: User enumeration › user search does not return other users' email addresses
cause: server/routes/users.ts:262 maps results through sanitizeUser (server/storage.ts:165), which only removes the password field — email and all other columns pass through.
fix: Return a public DTO from search (allow-list), not sanitizeUser.

title: Usernames/emails are unique only case-sensitively, enabling impersonation and per-mailbox duplicates
scenario: Attacker registers a case variant of a known user ('Alice' vs 'alice') to impersonate them.
evidence: register 'Dup<run>' -> 201; register 'dup<run>' -> 201. (Trailing-space variant is correctly rejected because the schema trims.)
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Account takeover and privilege escalation › usernames differing only in case are treated as the same (no case-variant impersonation)
cause: server/storage/user-storage.ts:47/66 use eq(users.username,…)/eq(users.email,…) (case-sensitive) and the DB unique constraints (shared/schema.ts) are on the raw text columns.
fix: Normalize email to lower case on write; compare usernames case-insensitively with a unique index on lower(username)/lower(email) and getUserByUsername/Email using lower(); keep display case for usernames.

title: Session cookie is not marked Secure behind the HTTPS reverse proxy
scenario: The session cookie can be sent over a downgraded/plain-HTTP request and captured.
evidence: GET /api/csrf-token with X-Forwarded-Proto: https (TRUST_PROXY=true) -> Set-Cookie: connect.sid=…; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax (no Secure).
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Session attacks › session cookie carries HttpOnly, SameSite and (behind an HTTPS proxy) Secure
cause: server/routes/index.ts:138 cookie.secure = process.env.REQUIRE_HTTPS === 'true', which defaults to false (docker-compose.yml/.env.example) although the documented deployment is nginx + TLS.
fix: Use cookie.secure: 'auto' (express-session honours X-Forwarded-Proto with trust proxy) or default REQUIRE_HTTPS to true in production.

title: No password strength policy — weak/common passwords are accepted
scenario: Users (and attackers creating throwaway accounts) set trivially guessable passwords like 'password'.
evidence: register with password 'password' (8 chars) -> 201. Only length is checked (min 8, max 128).
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Password policy › weak/common passwords are rejected
cause: shared/schema.ts:529 password: z.string().min(8).max(128) with no complexity/blocklist; updatePasswordSchema (shared/schema.ts) newPassword likewise min(8).
fix: Add a strength check (zxcvbn score threshold or a common-password blocklist) on both registration and password change.

title: Registration reveals whether a username or email is already taken (enumeration)
scenario: Attacker enumerates valid usernames/emails by observing distinct 400 messages at registration.
evidence: register existing username -> 400 'Username already exists'; register existing email -> 400 'Email already registered'. (Login itself does not leak ban status on a wrong password — that returns the generic 'Invalid username or password'.)
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: User enumeration › registering a taken username does not confirm it exists; › registering a taken email does not confirm it exists
cause: server/auth.ts:254-262 returns field-specific messages for duplicate username/email.
fix: Optional: return a generic error and (for email) send a 'that address is already registered' notice out-of-band; this is a usability/privacy trade-off.

title: INITIAL_OWNER bootstrap can be squatted: pre-registering the owner username blocks owner creation
scenario: On a fresh deployment, an attacker who registers the configured INITIAL_OWNER_USERNAME before first boot denies the operator their owner account (and keeps a normal account on that name).
evidence: Code reading: seedInitialOwner (server/db-migrations.ts:155-179) finds the existing account; because the password does not match and INITIAL_OWNER_RESET_PASSWORD is not set, it returns at :176-179 and does NOT promote it — the real owner is never created and the squatter keeps the username. Could not be reproduced automatically because the test DB is already bootstrapped (routeowner is owner).
test: tests/attacks/auth.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Account takeover and privilege escalation › INITIAL_OWNER bootstrap can be squatted ... (test.todo)
cause: server/db-migrations.ts:176-179 bails out silently when a same-named account exists with a different password; registration (server/auth.ts:248) is open and race-able before the operator's first boot.
fix: On a conflicting pre-existing account, log a loud warning and optionally refuse to start, or reserve configured owner usernames from public registration; document that INITIAL_OWNER should be seeded before opening registration.
